audience: Engineers with basic programming knowledge learning api server. Explain concepts directly and connect their mechanisms, consequences and design choices. Examples are optional when they clarify a concept; assessment does not require a recurring application, brand names or an example on every card.
prerequisites: A program runs instructions, holds data in memory and can call other code; separate processes do not automatically share their memory.
A network can carry messages between computers, and messages can be delayed or fail to arrive.
An HTTP request has a method, URL, headers and optional body; its response has a status, headers and optional body.
A client requests work from a server; a database stores data that an application can read and change.

objectives.description: Define the API server as application request-handling code and distinguish its responsibilities from client presentation and data storage.
Trace routing, input validation, identity and permission checks, application work and response construction.
Distinguish completing work in the request from accepting work for later processing and explain the separate completion signal.
Explain response-time benefits and the extra status, failure and duplicate-processing coordination caused by deferred work.
Explain the inside of an API server and choose immediate or deferred execution from the required response semantics.

questions.question: What is an API and what does an API server do? Distinguish its application responsibilities from client presentation and database storage, and explain whether every request must read or write a database. Trace an API request from arrival to response: explain routing, input validation, authentication, authorization, application logic and optional database or service calls. Distinguish authentication from authorization, and explain why invalid or disallowed requests must not perform the protected operation.
criteria: An API defines how software requests operations and interprets results; the API server implements those operations.
The server applies application rules and coordinates required work; clients present or consume results while databases manage stored data.
Some operations need stored data and others do not; the API server is not merely another name for a database.
Routing selects a handler; validation checks input shape and acceptable values before dependent work.
Authentication establishes identity; authorization checks permission for the specific operation or resource. An authenticated caller is not automatically authorized.
The handler performs allowed application work, uses dependencies as needed and returns a result or error; validation and permission failures prevent protected side effects.
criticalMisconceptions: Being signed in grants access to every resource.

questions.question: Compare finishing an operation before responding with accepting it for background processing. Define a queue and worker at the level needed for deferred work. Trace acceptance and eventual completion, explain how the caller learns the outcome, and state why an acceptance response does not prove completion. What can deferred work improve for a slow operation, and what does it not improve automatically? Explain status tracking, later failure reporting and retries, including how retrying uncertain work can duplicate an effect and why repeated processing needs a deliberate policy.
criteria: Immediate processing returns the operation's result after its required work; deferred processing returns an acceptance after arranging later work.
A queue holds pending work and a worker processes it later; acceptance and job completion are distinct events.
The caller needs a job identity and status lookup or notification to learn completion or failure; accepted work can still fail.
Deferral reduces how long the caller waits for acceptance and separates execution from that request; it does not automatically reduce total work or time to completion.
Status and result tracking must distinguish pending, successful and failed work, and later failures need a visible outcome.
Retries can recover transient failures but an uncertain previous attempt may have taken effect; duplicate-safe handling or explicit deduplication is needed for effects that must not repeat.
criticalMisconceptions: An accepted response means the background work is finished.
Moving work to a queue gives unlimited processing capacity or exactly-once effects.

questions.question: For a quick operation whose result is required immediately and a long operation whose caller can wait, choose immediate or deferred handling and justify each choice. For either design describe request validation, permission checks, dependencies, the response meaning and what happens if required work fails; state the coordination cost of your choice.
criteria: An immediate result requirement favors completing the necessary work before returning success; tolerance for later completion can justify acceptance plus background execution.
The design connects input and permissions to application work and dependencies, and defines success or acceptance accurately.
Failures have an explicit response or tracked job outcome; deferral adds queue/worker and status coordination, so it is chosen for a need rather than applied universally.
